newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Colombo port plans shipping service for Indian cargo.
newsitem.headline: Colombo port plans shipping service for Indian cargo.

text.p: Sri Lanka's state-owned ports and shipping organisations plan to launch a new feeder shipping service from Colombo port to attract more trans-shipment cargo from the Indian subcontinent, officials said on Tuesday.

"We want to set up a joint venture company with a foreign partner to start a new feeder service," a senior official of the state-run Ceylon Shipping Corporation said, adding that the Sri Lanka Port Authority would also be a partner in the venture.
"The idea is to promote Colombo as a trans-shipment port and divert Indian exports now moving via Singapore to Colombo," he told Reuters.
Colombo is already south Asia's hub for trans-shipment, an intermediate port where a vessel discharges cargo for reloading into another ship bound for the final destination.

Colombo, which handles 23 percent of cargo from the subcontinent, wants to raise its share of trans-shipment trade amid competition from ports like Singapore for increased volumes anticipated with the liberalisation of India's economy.
But some trans-shipment operators say Colombo, rather than increasing feeder services, needs to improve productivity and end berthing delays to have any hope of attracting more trade.

"The port is unable to accomodate existing feeders because of congestion and a shortage of cranes and prime movers," said Rohan Abeywickrema of Sea Consortium Lanka, the Indian Ocean island's biggest trans-shipment operator.
"To attract the subcontinent traffic the port should ensure connections between feeder vessels and main lines are met by providing berthing for feeders without delay," he told Reuters.
Five feeder services operate in Colombo with at least 60 feeder vessels calling at the port every month.
Shipping Ministry spokesman Daya Wijesekera disagreed with Abeywickrema. He said feeder ships faced berthing delays only when weather was bad but were otherwise given berths on arrival.
The port expects to install another gantry crane next year and has ordered three container transfer cranes as well as 39 prime movers, he said.
The sharp rise in trans-shipment in Colombo meant that productivity was not a major problem, he said.
Trans-shipment traffic in Colombo rose 48 percent in August to 97,288 containers from 65,721 containers in August 1995, Wijesekera said.
"We handled a total of 128,164 containers this August, the highest ever handled in a month," he said.

The Shipping Corporation official said Colombo wants to get more cargo from the subcontinent's eastern and western coasts, and especially from Calcutta and Chittagong, to make use of the port's under-utilised capacity, he added.
Colombo handled just over a million containers last year, up 7.9 per cent from 972,642 containers in 1994, although its capacity is 1.6 million containers.
